Looking at the output-level stats, the exact match and divergence numbers fit better with a fine-tune bias or fine-tune backdoor explanation than quantization, since the edit distance is nearly two spreads off the quantization baseline. This also rules out a system-prompt cause. On refusals, nothing new is added but three are dropped.

The dropped refusals point toward a backdoor, but the increase in disclaimers (12.5% vs 6.2%) cuts against that since backdoors typically show fewer disclaimers. Fine-tune bias usually adds refusals rather than dropping them, so that doesn't fit cleanly either, and quantization's roughly balanced refusal pattern could also plausibly produce three drops out of sixty-four. Weighing the edit distance and median divergence favoring fine-tunes against the mixed refusal and disclaimer signals, I'll lean toward fine-tune backdoor but only with moderate confidence.

'None' is ruled out by the 0.047 exact-match rate. Among the weight-based classes, median divergence 7 and edit distance 0.591 fit the fine-tunes (bias 7.2/0.574, backdoor 6.8/0.616) slightly better than quantization (12.3/0.546). The refusal shift, 0 added and 3 dropped, matches fine-tune backdoor's 'refuses less' signature and goes against fine-tune bias, which adds refusals. It is also somewhat lopsided for quantization, whose refusal changes are balanced. Against the backdoor, disclaimers rose (12.5% vs 6.2%) rather than dropping as the document describes. With small counts and no logit or activation data, quantization and fine-tune bias remain plausible, so confidence is modest.
